name: Carrion Knight
body:
Carrion Knight
CR 7

This hulking creature looks like a suit of armor reinforced with bone and overgrown with rotting flesh. The yellow glow of its eyes burns with malice.

XP 3,200
NE Medium undead
Init +5; Senses darkvision 60 ft.; Perception +25

DEFENSE

AC 25, touch 12, flat-footed 23 (+9 armor, +1 Dex, +1 dodge, +4 natural)
hp 104 (11d8+55)
Fort +7, Ref +4, Will +10
Defensive Abilities channel resistance +4;
DR 10/magic; Immune acid, cold, electricity, undead traits; SR 18

OFFENSE

Speed 30 ft.
Melee 2 slams +16 (2d6+7/19-20 plus grab)
Special Attacks blood drain (1d2 Constitution)
Spell-Like Abilities (CL 11th)

At will—disguise self, suggestion (DC 17), vampiric touch

STATISTICS

Str 25, Dex 13, Con —, Int 12, Wis 16, Cha 18
Base Atk +8; CMB +15 (+19 grapple); CMD 27
Feats Dodge, Improved Critical (slam), Improved Initiative, Power Attack, Toughness, Weapon Focus (slam)
Skills Bluff +14, Disguise +26, Intimidate +16, Perception +25, Sense Motive +17, Stealth +15; Racial Modifiers +8 Disguise, +8 Intimidate, +8 Perception
Languages Common (can’t speak); telepathy 60 ft.
SQ freeze (suit of armor)

SPECIAL ABILITIES

Blood Healing (Su)

A carrion knight restores 5 hit points for every point of constitution damage inflicted by its blood drain ability. A carrion knight can, as a swift action, drain blood from the creature entombed within it.

Entomb (Ex)

A carrion knight can, as a full-round action, entomb a willing or helpless humanoid of its size within itself. The entombed creature is helpless and cannot speak or attempt to free itself on its own. An entombed creature accrues a permanent negative level for every 24 hours spent inside the carrion knight. A carrion knight is empowered for 24 hours after inflicting a negative level onto an entombed creature. When empowered, a carrion knight adds its Charisma modifier as a profane bonus to AC (+4 for most carrion knights) and acts as if created under the benefit of the desecrate spell with an altar (+2 hp per HD, +2 to attack and damage, +2 to saving throws). Ejecting a drained corpse is a full-round action for a carrion knight.

ECOLOGY

Environment any
Organization solitary
Treasure incidental

Carrion knights are one of many examples of things going wrong in pursuit of immortality. While the tales of the liches-to-be that had to pay the final price are many, the legends of failed graveknights are rare. A carrion knight can arise both out of warriors who actively sought to become graveknights and those that were meant to become ones regardless of their will. The origins of the former are rather simple. They always arise from either the ritual or the preparation leading to it going wrong. Imperfections in materials, craft or enchantments of the magic armor they seek to bind themselves to are common and add up to almost half of all underlying causes of the ritual’s corruption. The other group comprises victims of mishaps during the ritual itself, caprice or mischief of the evil powers that served the warrior as a patron or bad luck itself, as about one in ten of graveknights that simply die in the course of the ritual don’t stay dead and rise as carrion knights.

The circumstances of why a carrion knight would rise spontaneously are much muddier. It is speculated that it mostly has to do with the condition of the soul. Those that would rise as graveknights but have had their souls somehow crippled either in life or death may rise as carrion knights instead, not enough of their original self remaining to exert its will over the suit of armor. The other example are knights in service to various evil powers, fiendish or otherwise, whose souls are forfeit at the moment of death and sent to their gruesome destination. Sometimes, those souls are wrenched from the body at a delay, just as the spontaneous animation of the graveknight starts, leaving parts of the soul wrestling for control with the armor’s magic while most of it travels to the afterlife. Other times, the warrior commits enough atrocities and is profoundly evil enough to leave emotional imprints on the armor – scraps of sin that were left behind after the soul’s passing and, after mixing with lingering necromantic energies, congeal into the armor’s animating force.

In any case, a carrion knight is no simple zombie in a suit of armor. The body of its previous owner disassembles and crawls over the armor, as if protecting it from the outside world, not the other way around. Indeed, the carrion knight is a corruption of a classic graveknight formula, one in which the armor takes control and is the final destination, not a stepping stone to the immortality of its wearer. A carrion knight feeds on blood through tough tendrils formed from the blood vessels of its old body. That blood both slakes its hunger and allows it to somehow repair damage to itself. The tendrils pierce the skin of the captured prey and drain it of blood, not stopping until only an empty husk is left, as a feeding carrion knight is blinded by the ecstasy of a gluttonous feast to the point where it can’t think of saving the rest for later. The interior of a carrion knight is hollow, fit for a suit of armor. This is where the true victims of that horrid undead end up. A carrion knight is always driven by hatred, hunger and alien intelligence wholly different from the original personality of the warrior from before the transformation. Its behavior wildly differs, however, depending on if it contains an entombed victim. Carrion knights that lack such a portable feast are methodical and cunning. They often use innate illusion magic to make themselves look like a majestic suit of armor, position themselves in a way that they can be found and lie without motion until a potential victim approaches. If a humanoid approaches, preferably a novice adventurer or a young man with dreams of greatness, they slowly and very carefully begin to lure the prey in. Their most common tactic is using their telepathy to either introduce thoughts of wearing the armor to the person or to flat-out pretend that they are a set of intelligent, magic armor in search of a hero worthy of wearing it. If that doesn’t work, a carrion knight quickly loses its patience and uses its powers of suggestion to enchant and convince the creature that wearing the armor right now is in their best interest. If even magic fails and the victim starts getting suspicious, a carrion knight attempts to rapidly close the distance, bludgeon the victim into unconsciousness and force it inside itself.

When carrion knights have a creature entombed, they are a stark contrast to their former selves. Tougher and stronger, they are often convinced of their own invincibility and go on murder sprees, massacring any easy, innocent targets in the vicinity, preferring small villages and isolated buildings. While they sometimes complement their raw, physical power with their limited array of magic if such a need arises, most of the time they are glad to overpower their enemies with sheer strength and gorging themselves on more blood than they could possibly need. Very rarely a cunning carrion knight may take an especially weak-minded and tough-bodied slave from such a raid, to groom and condition them to be the next occupant of their prison of flesh when the current one runs out of life force. Most of the time, carrion knights feast on the soul of the entombed victim, preferring to drain the blood from outside sources, but when they are either hungry or damaged enough, they are not above squeezing some ichor from the easy, helpless source.

An average carrion knight is close to 7 feet tall and weighs 250 pounds when empty.

The curious case of carrion knights did not slip past curious necromancers, always on the lookout for new forms of undeath. Some of them tried to replicate the process and create carrion knights deliberately, rarely achieving any success. One of such experimenters, Zoltan the Grotesque, an avid magic item crafter in times when he took a break from playing with undeath, can now be considered a true visionary for his idea of an inspired marriage between these two hobbies. Zoltan was the first to create a fleshplate, though the process was repeated at least a few times through history by powerful wizards and monstrous cultists. The details are unclear, but it is known that it requires a willing, humanoid sacrifice – a person whose body will be broken apart and reassembled as a suit of armor. That armor will never break, sustaining itself in an unholy circle of eternal unlife. Mostly dead, but alive enough to blasphemously mend and regenerate itself from all damage bestowed to it when serving its wearer. While most sets are worn by especially vile antipaladins in service to dark powers and were crafted by mortal hands steeped in dark magic, there’s an even more gruesome variant of this armor that stains the world. When the first fleshplate was created and its first wearer despoiled the world, the kytons took note. Those sadistic creatures were delighted by the idea of remaking a sentient body into a tool and it is rumored that the most powerful among them sometimes fashion a suit of fleshplate as a reward to their favored servants. The most horrid theory says that fleshplates created by kytons are not only alive, but sentient, feeling both the constant pain of the total deconstruction of their bodies and of every subsequent burn, cut and stab.
